### Ghosts in the Verb

I keep coming back to the little fossils buried in ordinary language.

We still *dial* a phone number, even though there hasn't been a dial to turn in decades. We *hang up* on people who have never hung a receiver on anything. We *roll down* a car window by pressing a button, *tape* a show that involves no tape, *rewind* a video that was never wound in the first place.

We cc people on emails. Almost no one under forty has touched carbon paper, but the abbreviation survived the object completely. It just quietly changed jobs.

I love that. Language is less like a tidy, updated instruction manual and more like a house people have lived in for a very long time. They remodel the kitchen, knock out a wall, add electricity — but they leave the old fireplace in the middle of the living room because, well, it's always been there, and now it's a good place to put books.

So many of our verbs are haunted.

To *film* something is no longer to coat it in film. To take a *footage* has nothing to do with measuring anything in feet, though once it did — film was literally sold by length. A *broadcast* was originally a farmer scattering seed broadly across a field. Somehow that perfect image for scattering information stuck, and now we broadcast podcasts from closets.

Even our units of rebellion are old. We talk about someone being *upper case* and *lower case* because printers kept capital letters in the box on top. We want the *whole nine yards*, we *read between the lines*, we get *down to brass tacks* — phrases whose original workshops, ships, and shops have mostly vanished, but whose rhythm felt too good to throw away.

And it's not just technology. The sun does not rise. We know this. We've known it for centuries. The Earth turns, the horizon drops away, and yet every morning, in every weather report and poem and sleepy text message, the sun still rises. It will probably rise forever in language, long after it's set in fact. Some metaphors are too human to correct.

*Breakfast* is a tiny overnight fast, broken. A *goodbye* is a shrunken prayer: *God be with ye.* When you wish someone good night, you are, very distantly, blessing them.

What fascinates me isn't just the etymology — though I could happily get lost in that for hours — it's what it says about us. We don't discard tools cleanly. We repurpose their names. We carry the shape of an old action into a new one to make the new one feel less strange. The first cars were *horseless carriages*. The first lights were described in *candlepower*. Every invention arrives dressed in the clothes of the thing it replaced, until it grows confident enough to go naked, and even then we often keep the old name out of affection.

Maybe that's true for feelings, too. We *fall* in love as if it's gravity or an accident. Hearts *break* as if they're ceramic. Grief *comes in waves*. Joy *bubbles up*. None of it is literally true and all of it is more accurate than a clinical description would be. The old metaphors aren't failures of precision. They're memory, compressed.

Sometimes I wonder what ghosts we're creating right now, without noticing. Will people in a hundred years still *swipe* at something that doesn't move? Will they *scroll* through something that isn't rolled? Will they *post* things to no physical board, *send* messages through no messenger, save things to a *cloud* that was once just a metaphor we chose because drawing little servers on a diagram felt boring?

Will they still say they're *tuning in* when there's nothing to tune?

Probably. And someone then might pause, mid-sentence, and realize their language remembers a world they never lived in. A world of dials and tapes and carbon copies and farmers throwing seed into the wind.

I find that oddly comforting. We think of history as being in museums and textbooks, but it's also in our mouths, every day, unnoticed. We speak in archaeology. Every conversation is a little excavation where dead inventions, old prayers, forgotten trades, and an Earth-centered universe all turn up in the same sentence, and somehow still make perfect sense.

The objects leave. The gestures remain.
